<reason>A built the debate around the motion's own constraints — the 2026–2036 window and the verb "reduce" — and pressed both relentlessly. The Q1 pressure question forced B to concede new-build contributes essentially zero in-window generation, gutting half the proposition as literally worded. A then exploited B's own "avoided increase" framing by pointing out the counterfactual (gas backfill) is increasingly outdated as B itself conceded closures are now backfilled by clean sources, building a clean dilemma in closing: either the stale gas counterfactual (undefended) or a clean-backfill world where extension buys zero incremental tons. B fought well — the pressure question exposing A's factual error about outage length ("dark plant") was well-executed and honestly answered by A, and B's late opportunity-cost/portfolio argument (extension frees renewable dollars from a "backfill detour" toward direct fossil displacement) was the strongest unaddressed thread B produced. But A's closing partially neutralized it by reframing nuclear as merely an "enabler" rather than a "reducer," and B never fully rebutted A's core temporal-accounting attack or recovered from conceding away the new-build half of its own case. Overall A kept tighter discipline on the motion's actual wording and left B defending a narrower, more qualified version of the proposition.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure-question pair (Q1 on the "dark plant" claim, Q2 on the closure-contradiction) was the sharpest tactical strike, forcing a real concession from A — but A's subsequent fork in closing (gas-backfill vs. clean-backfill dilemma), built directly on that exchange, was the more decisive move because B's closing portfolio argument couldn't fully escape it before the debate ended.</best_rebuttal>
